Compare the 3 Cloud Deployment Models: Cloud, Hybrid, and On-Premises.
column2:
Cloud (Cloud-Native): Fully deployed in AWS.
Hybrid: Connects on-premises infrastructure/apps with AWS cloud resources (e.g., via VPN, Direct Connect, Outposts, Storage Gateway).
On-Premises (Private Cloud): Deployed locally in your own data center using virtualization/resource tools.

column1: Compare the 4 main ways to interact with and provision AWS services: Console, CLI, SDK, and IaC.
column2:
AWS Management Console: Web GUI for visual/one-time tasks.
AWS CLI: Terminal scripts/automation.
AWS SDK: Calling AWS APIs inside application code (Python, Java, JS, etc.).
IaC (CloudFormation): Declarative repeatable templates for entire environments.

column1: Define AWS Regions, Availability Zones (AZs), and Edge Locations.
column2:
Region: Physical geographic area with 3+ isolated AZs.
Availability Zone (AZ): 1+ discrete data centers with redundant power/networking inside a Region (isolated from other AZ failures).
Edge Location: Global PoP used by CloudFront and Route 53 to cache/serve content with ultra-low latency.

column1: What are the 4 main factors to consider when choosing an AWS Region?
column2:
1. Compliance / Data Sovereignty laws
2. Proximity / Low Latency to end users
3. Available AWS services & features
4. Pricing differences between Regions

column1: When should you deploy across Multiple AZs vs. Multiple Regions?
column2:
Multi-AZ: Standard High Availability within one Region (no single point of failure).
Multi-Region: Disaster recovery / business continuity against regional outages, global low latency, or data sovereignty requirements.

column1: What are AWS Outposts, AWS Local Zones, and AWS Wavelength?
column2:
Outposts: AWS-managed hardware racks installed in your on-premises data center.
Local Zones: Extensions of an AWS Region placed close to major metro areas for single-digit ms latency.
Wavelength: AWS compute/storage embedded inside 5G telecom carrier networks for mobile edge apps.

column1: Match Amazon EC2 instance families to workloads: General Purpose, Compute, Memory, Accelerated, Storage Optimized.
column2:
General Purpose (T, M): Balanced web/app servers.
Compute Optimized (C): CPU-heavy batch, HPC, gaming.
Memory Optimized (R, X): In-memory databases/caches.
Accelerated Computing (P, G): GPUs/ML training/graphics.
Storage Optimized (I, D): High sequential I/O local NVMe/NoSQL.

column1: What do Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling accomplish together?
column2:
ELB: Automatically distributes incoming traffic across healthy targets in multiple AZs (ALB = HTTP/HTTPS L7; NLB = ultra-fast TCP/UDP L4).
Auto Scaling: Automatically adds/removes EC2 instances based on demand/health checks for elasticity and fault tolerance.

column1: What is AWS Lambda?
column2: Event-driven serverless compute service that runs your code in response to events without provisioning or managing servers — you pay only for requests and compute duration (max 15 min per execution).

column1: Compare Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, Amazon ECR, and AWS Fargate.
column2:
ECS: AWS-native container orchestration.
EKS: Managed Kubernetes orchestration.
ECR: Fully managed Docker/OCI container image registry.
Fargate: Serverless compute engine for ECS/EKS containers (no EC2 nodes to manage).

column1: What is AWS Elastic Beanstalk?
column2: Platform as a Service (PaaS) — upload your web application code and Elastic Beanstalk automatically handles provisioning, load balancing, auto scaling, and health monitoring (underlying EC2/resources remain accessible).

column1: What is Amazon Lightsail?
column2: Easy-to-use virtual private server (VPS) service with simple, predictable fixed monthly pricing — ideal for small websites, WordPress blogs, simple dev environments, and beginners.

column1: What is AWS Batch?
column2: Fully managed service that dynamically provisions optimal compute resources to run hundreds of thousands of batch computing jobs (no need to install/manage batch scheduling software).

column1: What is AWS CloudFormation?
column2: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) service that uses repeatable JSON or YAML templates to model and provision AWS (and third-party) resources consistently across Regions and accounts.

column1: What is AWS Systems Manager (SSM)?
column2: Operational hub to view and control AWS and hybrid infrastructure at scale — includes Patch Manager (OS patching), Session Manager (secure shell without SSH keys/open port 22), Run Command, and Parameter Store.

column1: What is AWS Service Catalog?
column2: Allows organizations to create and manage a curated catalog of pre-approved IT services/CloudFormation templates so teams can self-service deploy compliant resources safely.

column1: Define Amazon VPC, Subnets, Internet Gateway (IGW), and NAT Gateway.
column2:
VPC: Logically isolated virtual network in AWS.
Public vs. Private Subnet: Public routes to an IGW; Private has no direct inbound internet access.
IGW: Connects a VPC to the public internet.
NAT Gateway: Allows private subnet instances outbound internet access while blocking inbound internet traffic.

column1: Compare Security Groups vs. Network ACLs (NACLs) in Amazon VPC.
column2:
Security Group: Instance/ENI level, stateful (return traffic auto-allowed), Allow rules only.
NACL: Subnet level, stateless (must explicitly allow inbound & outbound), supports both Allow and Deny rules evaluated in numbered order.

column1: What is Amazon Route 53?
column2: Highly available, scalable cloud DNS web service (100% availability SLA) providing domain registration, DNS routing (latency, geolocation, failover, weighted), and health checking.

column1: What is Amazon CloudFront?
column2: Global Content Delivery Network (CDN) that caches static and dynamic web content (HTML, images, video, APIs) at worldwide Edge Locations to reduce latency and offload origin servers.

column1: What is AWS Global Accelerator?
column2: Networking service that routes global TCP/UDP user traffic over the AWS private global backbone using 2 static Anycast IP addresses for improved performance and fast regional failover (no content caching).

column1: Compare AWS Site-to-Site VPN, AWS Client VPN, and AWS Direct Connect.
column2:
Site-to-Site VPN: Encrypted IPsec tunnel over public internet (fast setup, low cost).
Client VPN: Managed VPN for individual remote users/laptops.
Direct Connect: Dedicated private physical fiber connection (consistent high bandwidth, low latency, weeks to provision, not encrypted by default).

column1: What are AWS Transit Gateway and AWS PrivateLink?
column2:
Transit Gateway: Central hub-and-spoke network router simplifying connections among many VPCs and on-premises networks.
PrivateLink: Provides private connectivity between VPCs, AWS services, and SaaS/partner services without traversing the public internet.

column1: What is Amazon API Gateway?
column2: Fully managed service to create, publish, maintain, monitor, and secure REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs at any scale (often serves as the serverless front door to AWS Lambda).

column1: What is Amazon S3 and what are its core characteristics?
column2: Unlimited regional object storage designed for 11 9s (99.999999999%) durability across multiple AZs, supporting static website hosting, versioning, encryption, and automated lifecycle policies.

column1: Summarize the main Amazon S3 Storage Classes by access pattern and cost.
column2:
Standard: Frequent access.
Intelligent-Tiering: Unknown/changing access (auto-moves, small monitoring fee).
Standard-IA / One Zone-IA: Infrequent, rapid ms access (One Zone = 1 AZ, cheaper, re-creatable data).
Glacier Instant / Flexible / Deep Archive: Archival (ms / min-hrs / 12-48h lowest cost, 180d min).

column1: Compare Amazon EBS vs. EC2 Instance Store.
column2:
Amazon EBS: Persistent network-attached block storage volumes in 1 AZ; survives EC2 stop/start; supports snapshots to S3.
Instance Store: Ephemeral high-speed local NVMe disk physically attached to host; data is lost on stop, hibernate, or terminate.

column1: Compare Amazon EFS vs. Amazon FSx.
column2:
Amazon EFS: Serverless, elastic, POSIX-compliant Linux NFS shared file system mountable across multiple AZs simultaneously.
Amazon FSx: Managed third-party file systems including Windows File Server (SMB), Lustre (HPC), NetApp ONTAP, and OpenZFS.

column1: What are AWS Storage Gateway, AWS Backup, and AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)?
column2:
Storage Gateway: Hybrid bridge giving on-prem apps low-latency access to AWS cloud storage (File, Volume, Tape).
AWS Backup: Centralized automated backup policy management across AWS services.
Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS): Continuous block-level replication for rapid recovery of on-prem/cloud servers into AWS.

column1: What is Amazon RDS, and how do Multi-AZ Deployments differ from Read Replicas?
column2:
RDS: Managed relational SQL database (MySQL, Postgres, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server).
Multi-AZ: Synchronous standby replica in another AZ for High Availability / automatic failover.
Read Replicas: Asynchronous copies to offload and scale read performance.

column1: What is Amazon Aurora?
column2: AWS cloud-native MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible relational database offering up to 5x MySQL / 3x PostgreSQL throughput, auto-scaling storage up to 128 TB, and 6 copies replicated across 3 AZs.

column1: What is Amazon DynamoDB?
column2: Fully managed, serverless NoSQL (key-value & document) database delivering consistent single-digit millisecond latency at any scale with zero server management.

column1: Compare Amazon ElastiCache, Amazon DocumentDB, and Amazon Neptune.
column2:
ElastiCache: Sub-millisecond in-memory caching (Valkey/Redis/Memcached) to accelerate read-heavy apps.
DocumentDB: Managed MongoDB-compatible JSON document database.
Neptune: Managed Graph database for highly connected data (social graphs, fraud detection, recommendations).

column1: What are AWS DMS (Database Migration Service) and AWS SCT (Schema Conversion Tool)?
column2:
AWS DMS: Migrates databases to AWS quickly with minimal downtime (source DB stays live during migration).
AWS SCT: Converts database schemas/code when migrating between different engines (heterogeneous), such as Oracle to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL.

column1: Compare Amazon Redshift, Amazon Athena, and Amazon EMR.
column2:
Redshift: Petabyte-scale SQL data warehouse (OLAP) for complex BI analytics.
Athena: Serverless interactive SQL queries directly on Amazon S3 data (pay per TB scanned).
EMR: Managed big data platform running Apache Hadoop & Spark clusters.

column1: Compare AWS Glue, Amazon Kinesis, Amazon OpenSearch Service, and Amazon Quick.
column2:
AWS Glue: Serverless ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) and data catalog.
Kinesis: Ingest and process real-time streaming data.
OpenSearch: Log analytics, real-time monitoring, and full-text search.
Amazon Quick (formerly QuickSight): Serverless BI dashboards and data visualization.

column1: What are Amazon SageMaker AI and Amazon Q?
column2:
Amazon SageMaker AI (updated 2026 name): End-to-end platform for data scientists/devs to build, train, and deploy ML & foundation models.
Amazon Q: Generative AI assistant for business knowledge queries, coding, and AWS operations.

column1: Match AWS Language & Document AI Services: Comprehend, Textract, Transcribe, Polly, Translate.
column2:
Comprehend: NLP sentiment & entity extraction from text.
Textract: OCR extracting text, tables, and forms from scanned PDFs/images.
Transcribe: Speech-to-Text.
Polly: Text-to-Lifelike Speech.
Translate: Neural language translation.

column1: Match AWS Vision & Conversational Services: Amazon Rekognition, Amazon Lex, and Amazon Connect.
column2:
Rekognition: Image & video analysis (faces, objects, content moderation).
Lex: Build conversational AI voice & text chatbots (tech behind Alexa).
Connect: Cloud-based omnichannel contact / call center service.

column1: Compare Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Step Functions.
column2:
SQS: Managed message queue (pull-based) to decouple microservices.
SNS: Managed pub/sub notification service (push fan-out to email, SMS, SQS, Lambda).
EventBridge: Serverless event bus routing AWS/custom/SaaS events.
Step Functions: Visual serverless workflow orchestration (state machines).

column1: Compare AWS CodeBuild, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS X-Ray.
column2:
CodeBuild: Fully managed build service that compiles code, runs tests, and produces packages.
CodePipeline: Managed CI/CD orchestrator automating build, test, and deploy stages.
X-Ray: Distributed tracing to debug and analyze latency across microservices.

column1: Compare Amazon WorkSpaces, Amazon AppStream 2.0, and Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser.
column2:
WorkSpaces: Managed persistent cloud virtual desktops (VDI).
AppStream 2.0: Streams specific desktop applications securely into any web browser.
WorkSpaces Secure Browser (formerly WorkSpaces Web): Managed secure browser access to internal websites & SaaS apps.

column1: What are Amazon SES, AWS Amplify, and AWS IoT Core?
column2:
Amazon SES: Cost-effective, scalable email sending/receiving service (transactional & marketing email).
AWS Amplify: Tools to build, deploy, and host frontend web & mobile apps rapidly.
AWS IoT Core: Securely connects billions of IoT devices to AWS cloud services.

column1: What are AWS Application Discovery Service, Migration Evaluator, AWS Application Migration Service (MGN), and AWS Migration Hub?
column2:
Application Discovery Service: Collects on-prem server specs & dependencies.
Migration Evaluator: Builds data-driven business case / TCO estimates.
Application Migration Service (MGN): Automates lift-and-shift (Rehost) server migration.
Migration Hub: Single dashboard tracking migration progress across tools.

column1: What is Amazon CloudWatch vs. AWS CloudTrail?
column2:
CloudWatch: Performance & operational monitoring (metrics like CPU utilization, logs, dashboards, alarms, auto-scaling triggers).
CloudTrail: Security & governance auditing (records who made which AWS API call, when, and from where).
